AI translation vs human translators: how accurate is AI translation?

November 21, 2023
Machine Translation | Translation agency | Translation Service Providers

Tools such as Google Translate, DeepL and ChatGPT now translate text in seconds, and most people in business have used at least one of them. The practical question is no longer whether AI translation works, but how accurate it is for the document in front of you and what happens if it gets something wrong.

The honest answer depends on the content. AI translation is a strong tool for some jobs and a risky one for others, and the difference is worth understanding before you put your name to a translated page, contract or customer message.

Where AI translation works well

AI translation is useful when speed matters more than polish and the cost of an error is low. You can use it to get the gist of a supplier email, to scan a foreign-language article or to draft internal notes that a colleague will check.

It also helps professionals. Many translators use machine translation as a first draft and then edit it, a process called post-editing. The international standard ISO 18587 sets out requirements for full human post-editing of machine translation output and for the competences of the people who do it, which shows that the industry treats the human step as a quality requirement, not an optional extra.

How accurate AI translation is

There is no single accuracy figure, because results vary by language pair, subject and style of writing. The best evidence comes from studies that test specific tools on specific documents.

One often-cited example comes from healthcare. In a 2019 study published in JAMA Internal Medicine, researchers at the University of California, San Francisco tested Google Translate on emergency department discharge instructions. At sentence level, 92% of the Spanish translations and 81% of the Chinese translations were accurate. Of all the sentences tested, 2% of the Spanish and 8% of the Chinese had the potential for clinically significant harm.

That study used an older system, and tools have improved since. It still shows the pattern that matters for business: output that reads fluently can contain errors that change meaning, and the reader may not notice. Accuracy can also differ sharply between languages, as the gap between Spanish and Chinese in that study shows.

Contextual understanding and consistency

Human language offers many valid options, and the right one depends on context. Idioms, humour, slogans and implied meaning rarely map word for word onto another language, so a literal rendering can be technically correct and still wrong for your reader.

Consistency is another weak spot. In a user manual, a contract or a set of product pages, each key term must be translated the same way every time. A human translator works from a glossary and style guide, and checks the whole document against them.

Different text types also call for different methods. A sworn translation, a legal contract, a travel brochure and a technical manual each follow their own conventions. BeTranslated’s team of specialist translators works in a wide range of fields, so your documents go to someone who knows the subject.

Cultural sensitivity and brand voice

When you translate marketing, the aim is for your audience to feel that the message was written for them. That means adapting references, tone, imagery and sometimes the whole idea, a process known as localisation or transcreation.

AI tools translate what the text says. They do not know your brand, your market or what a particular phrase suggests to a UK, French or Korean customer, unless a person supplies and checks that knowledge. For campaigns, slogans and website copy, a specialist marketing translator protects your reputation.

Certified translations, legal documents and UK rules

Some documents need more than an accurate translation. They need a person who takes responsibility for it.

Home Office visa applications, for example, require a certified translation of any document not in English or Welsh. The translator must confirm that the translation is accurate and include the date, their full name and signature, and their contact details. Companies House asks for a certified English translation when accounts are prepared in another language. An AI tool cannot provide that statement of accountability.

If your work involves legal documents, medical records or regulated financial information, a qualified human translator should translate or at least review the text.

Confidentiality and data protection

When you paste a document into a public AI tool, you are sharing its content with a third party. The Information Commissioner’s Office advises that UK data protection law covers personal data broadly, including data processed incidentally, and that organisations using third-party AI tools should understand what data they share and how the provider uses it.

Names, addresses, health details and commercial secrets are all easy to include by accident. A professional translation agency works under confidentiality terms and controls who sees your files, which gives you a clear process to rely on if you are ever asked where your data went.

Multilingual chatbots and your sales strategy

AI has also moved into customer conversations. Chatbots can now answer in many languages, which opens your website to visitors who would otherwise leave. For an online business, that can mean support outside office hours and fewer lost enquiries.

The risks are real, though. In February 2024, a tribunal in British Columbia ruled that Air Canada was responsible for inaccurate information its website chatbot gave a customer about bereavement fares, and ordered the airline to pay compensation. The decision came from a small-claims tribunal rather than a court, but it makes a point that applies to any business: you are accountable for what your chatbot tells customers, in every language it speaks.

If you plan to use a multilingual chatbot, treat the content as seriously as your website. Have professional linguists translate and review the knowledge base, key scripts and product terminology. Keep a glossary so the bot uses the same terms as your sales team, and give customers an easy route to a human adviser for anything complex.

Why automated AI translation can cost more

An error in a translated contract, product label or ad can lead to rework, returns, lost sales or a legal dispute. The saving on the translation itself disappears quickly if you have to fix and re-issue the material, or if it damages trust with a customer.

Use AI for low-risk, internal work. Use a human translator when the text represents your company, binds you legally or affects someone’s health, money or safety. If you are unsure which category your project falls into, ask us.

Tell us about your content, including any preference about the use of AI tools in the workflow, and request a free, no-obligation quote.

Frequently asked questions

How accurate is AI translation?

Accuracy varies by language pair, subject and text type. A 2019 University of California, San Francisco study found 92% sentence-level accuracy for Spanish and 81% for Chinese in medical discharge instructions, with some errors that could cause harm.

Will AI replace human translators?

AI has changed how translators work, and many use it for first drafts. Certified, legal, medical and brand-critical work still needs a qualified person who checks the result and accepts responsibility for it.

Can I use ChatGPT or Google Translate for business documents?

You can use them for internal drafts and to understand the gist of a text. For anything customer-facing, legal or regulated, have a professional translate or review it, and avoid pasting confidential or personal data into public tools.

Is AI translation accepted for UK visa applications?

Home Office applications need a certified translation for documents not in English or Welsh. That means a translator confirms the accuracy and provides their name, signature, date and contact details, which AI output cannot supply.

What is machine translation post-editing?

Post-editing is when a human linguist reviews and corrects machine translation output. ISO 18587 sets requirements for full human post-editing, and it suits some content types better than others, so ask your agency which workflow fits your project.
